"Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You" has a novel approach to the adventure/mystery game format, where the gameplay of highlighting the Internet history of People of Interest feels natural and the themes of modern surveillance fits like a glove. I recommend it to fans of story rich adventure/mystery games and people interested in media discussing state surveillance.

In Orwell, just as you can find the "right" perpetrator with the extreme access to personal information, the gameplay also showcases how that power to secretly surveil is just as capable of destroying lives. AAA games like the "Watch_Dogs" series have attempted to grapple with the same subject matter, but invariably it is portrayed as a superpower for a modern action hero. This feels like a much more grounded and mature take on epistemic injustice.

Flawed, but generally interesting game that mostly achieves what it sets out to do. A bit too heavy-handed and naive at times, could use a lot more subtlety and grey morality to it. It ends up feeling like a dressed-up visual novel, when it could've benefitted more from a free-form approach to solving its conundrums instead of a kind of linear path through an interface that pretends really hard that it's not a secret dialogue tree.

It's a very good game, at first I thought this is going to be some sort of "watching" simulator, with no real impact on story nor characters, but it turned out to be a complete opposite. Choices you make in this piece are not only impactful, but also very frequent and it's often difficult to foresee the consequences of your judgement. 
When it comes to the plot, it's not unbelievably complex and mind-blowing, but it definetely does its job in terms of being a solid foundation for players' interactions and decisions. After all, the key element in storyline's progression is you, so whatever happens inside of the game just remember that it wouldn't be here if it wasn't for you. I also liked character development and lore building, creating all of this information probably wasn't easy considering that the game has only 5 episodes and finishing them require, on average, something between 3 to 4 hours. 
Gameplay is honestly very enjoyable, it's kind of like a browsing/copy&paste simulator with decent layout and a pretty easy to use interface. What I enjoyed the most about it, was how well the creators of Orwell managed to make texts, phone calls and social media pages look very natural, almost like in real world, which is really immersive at the same time.
Overall, it's a very decent game and considering the fact that it's not a triple A title it's a 𝟲,𝟱/𝟭𝟬

I immediately purchased this after playing the demo. I got a 25% discount through the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/bundle/6251/Orwell_Seasons_Complete_Edition/][b]Orwell Seasons Complete Edition Bundle[/b][/url], but I think it's worth the full price even when purchased by itself. This kind of gameplay truly appeals to me. I love the information gathering and analysis process, as well as the user interface. 

I very much enjoyed following the conversations and checking out posts; sifting through the data and remapping the profiles while trying to anticipate the next moves based on possible hidden agenda was very exciting! (I know this is very vague, but I'm trying to avoid spoilers.)

I loved that they splurged on the details. They had advertisements on websites and also had weather and news panels on the menu. There were even red herrings! Although they were unnecessary to move forward with the investigation, they were entertaining and helped flesh out the world even more.

I also really appreciate that this game allowed me to enjoy the themes presented in its book inspiration, [b]1984[/b], even though I struggled with reading it. [i](I'm sorry, [b]Eric Arthur Blair †[/b], but I have to be real.)[/i] 

I [b]HIGHLY RECOMMEND[/b] this to people who enjoy cyber, investigative, and detective games set in a dystopian world presented through point & click and visual novel styles. 

Thank you so much for this game, [b]Osmotic Studios[/b]! I look forward to your next release—perhaps a new season of Orwell or maybe even a different game!

This is a game based on the concepts of George Orwell's '1984' novel, a novel about totalitarianism where a population has little to no freedom for the state's population. 

You are an investigator, led by an adviser, working for a government agency called "Orwell" with their main focus being to intercept some of "The Nation's" inhabitants. Specifically, you are tasked with solving the major catastrophe that the game is revolved around. You unearth many sensitive pieces of information and ultimately have some decisions to make.

[b]Completionist time (100%):[/b] 6-8hrs
[b]Overall rating:[/b] 8/10

[b]Pros[/b]
+60FPS
+Good story
+Investigation was fun
+Interesting low polygon art style
+Clean UI
+Soundtrack

[b]Cons[/b]
+Lots of hand holding
+Several bugs (one big one hovering over datachunks)
+Phone calls and texts take too long to finish

An interesting game that has you in control of a “Big Brother” surveillance system named Orwell. You must find out who or what is behind several violent attacks on a city. As you go through the story you must upload information you deem important (or fake info to throw Orwell off). Emails, texts, phone calls, computers, websites, etc. it’s all available to search through and piece the puzzle together. There is a lot of reading, but the info you can upload will get highlighted automatically. Sometimes there are conflicting pieces of information and you’ll need to decide what to upload.

The story is good with some twists and turns. It does have several endings and outcomes depending on your choices throughout each day. The gameplay is very straightforward and you can dumb it down to dragging things from one side of the screen to another until things happen. If you get into the game, it feels more than simply drag and drop. I found myself pausing and thinking things through, second guessing, regretting some uploads, etc. 

I did come across a rather annoying bug which seems to be common when looking at the discussions. Seemingly at random, when you hover over a highlighted piece of information it will not show you the summary of what gets uploaded to Orwell. This is a huge bummer because then you are uploading information that you may think one thing but the game thinks another. Sometimes logging out and going to the main menu fixes it, but not always. 


[b]Conclusion[/b]
I went back and played through it a second time to see different outcomes and to get all of the achievements. I enjoyed my time with the game and would recommend it on sale.

[b]6/10[/b] Above Average

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

After that, I can't say much without spoiling something, so either buy it or give the demo a try.

Essentially presents the counter-argument to "I have nothing to hide" in game form, and it does so brilliantly.

The game is set up so that you look through documents and conversations and can present evidence to your adviser who can't see what you see. In this way you can include bits and pieces of information to shape the narrative however you want by taking things out of context or choosing not to send pertinent information. In doing, so an innocuous statement can be construed as proof of wrongdoing, and lies can be presented as evidence without sending the actual facts. In other words, you can choose to send innocent people to jail and let criminals go free if you so wish merely by the power of suggestion.

The only negative in the presentation is that in multiple playthroughs you can't fast forward or skip conversations. The game is short enough that I was willing to sit through them, and you can multi-task by starting conversations then looking at other things, but it would have been nice to save a few minutes here and there.
NSA Prism Simulator!

The technology displayed in Orwell is already out there, though it's not called Orwell. And it's much more sophisticated. Whether you're a government agency, an intelligence agency or just someone powerful who has the ability to tap into the right resources, the data are out there. Government records, bank records, phone tracking, social media, internet activity, etc. It's already here and it's not that hard to piece together. Obviously, this is just a game, so it's perfectly understandable why Orwell isn't as sophisticated.

So, we live in a very terrifying world, it seems... but this game actually made me realise it's not as grim as it looks like. The concepts and warnings of this game, given the state of our society and the in-game characters, actually fall flat and, like I said, make you realise it's not that bad. Was that the intention, I wonder.

Why? Well, the majority of the monitored characters are either massive jerks (Cassandra and Harrison) or dangerous and certainly deserving investigation (I've already spoiled too much). And investigation isn't necessarily a bad thing. Even before the information age, there were detectives and police officers investigating crimes and stuff. The thing is about finding the right balance, I guess, but that's out of the scope if this game and its message.

Before this game, these things always worried me and I always thought about the impact on us all. Innocents caught and crushed between the merciless cogs of surveillance and false illusion of freedom. However, I failed to take into account that it's not just those behind those tools that are jerks. It's also those who end up between those cogs. So hey, maybe it's not so grim after all.

Like that line in the 1984 book about imagining the future -- a boot stamping on a human face, forever. If that face belongs to a jerk, then it's actually kinda good. True, innocent people will still get caught between the cogs, but at least it's not 100% just innocents. It probably is more like just 10% of the time. Cool. Thank you, Orwell, I guess I can sleep better at night today. :)

[h1] "Arguing that you don't care about the right to privacy because you have nothing to hide is no different than saying you don't care about free speech because you have nothing to say." - Edward Snowden [/h1]

[b]Spoiler-free review. You should play the prologue before buying it. [/b]

[b]Hours played at the time of review: 12.6 hours[/b]
[b]Game progress:[/b] [u]Achievements weren't difficult to do[/u], just had to play the chapters two and rarely 3 times. It might sound daunting BUT [u]with almost every achievement you get to know a bit more about the story[/u] so it is rewarding. 

[b]Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Opens up conversations about the future of our society
[*] 5 chapters, each one with twists and turns
[*] Memorable moments
[*] Multiple DIFFERENT endings
[/list]

[b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Not a particularly variant soundtrack
[*] No major consequence choices except one or two before the ending.
[*] No clue button to help you. Sometimes I got stuck in some places where I accidentally glanced over something.
[/list]

[b]The story and the gameplay[/b]
is about you investigating a bombing and trying to find out who did it. At the start, I felt a bit lost in the wrong way but I soon found myself immersed in the game. You have to move data chunks (specific words sometimes whole sentences) and upload it into Orwell; the secret tool that can pry into [i]anyone's[/i] private life. The gameplay is similar to Hypnospace Outlaw: You will have to [u]search through websites, chats, phone calls, computers and emails[/u] to find out who did the attack. You don't have to read everything to make bad decisions because [u]this game relies on YOUR moral compass and investigating skills[/u] in terms of what to upload.

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]

I got this game for free in a giveaway back when chrono was a thing, but I never actually played it until somewhat recently. Honestly, it is really good, and the story twisted in ways I never would have expected. If you're interested in games that emphasize narrative or if you just like dystopian stories of any sort, you should check out the demo and buy this if you like it. It's a bit of a short-lived experience, but it is well worth it, doubly so on sale, and triply so if you manage to win it in a random giveaway :p

Let's face it, games are not quite on par with books and TV series in terms of their narrative. So usually when people say a game has very good writing, they mean "for a game". This one has very good writing, period.
